title: Types of Vectors
notes: A zero vector has magnitude zero and no direction. It is the resultant of two equal and opposite vectors. Adding it to a vector leaves that vector unchanged.
A unit vector has magnitude 1 and points in a chosen direction. If A is a non-zero vector, the unit vector along it is Â = A / |A|. The symbols î, ĵ and k̂ are unit vectors along the coordinate axes.

Equal vectors have the same magnitude and the same direction. They need not act at the same point. A negative of a vector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction. Multiplying by −1 produces it.
Collinear vectors lie along the same line or along parallel lines. Like collinear vectors point the same way. Unlike collinear vectors point opposite ways.
A position vector of a point is drawn from the chosen origin to that point. It locates the point. A displacement vector joins two positions and does not have to start at the origin.

A free vector may be drawn anywhere provided its magnitude and direction stay the same. A force on a rigid body is not completely free, because its line of action decides the torque. The class keeps that distinction when moments are being calculated.
